result.topic_en: Riemann's excerpts in English from Locke's Essay Concerning Human Understanding, Book II, Chapter 21 (Of Power), on liberty, volition, the will and uneasiness as what determines the will, under a German heading on freedom and determinism.
result.transcription:
Über Freiheit und Determinismus[?]. Locke. Book II Chap. 21. [-§.4 cc-] §.5. cc
§.31[?] „Uneasiness determines the will". §.37.. Because that alone is present, and 'tis against the Nature of
Things, that what is absent should operate, where it is not.
„Liberty, what"
§.8. All the Actions, that we have any Idea of, reducing themselves, as has been said to these two
viz. Thinking and Motion; so far as a Man has a power to think, or not to think; to move, or
not to move, according to the Preference or Direction of his own Mind, so far is a Man free.
„Supposes the Understanding and Will" §.9. (§.15. Preferring, which seems perhaps best to
express the Act of Volition, does it not precisely. For though a Man would prefer
Flying to Walking yet who[?] can say he ever wills it? Volition, 'tis plain is an Act of the
Mind, knowingly exerting that Dominion it takes it self to have over any Part of the Man
by imploying it in, or with-holding it from any particular Action. And what is Will, but the
Faculty to do this) „Belongs not to Volition" §.10–13. „belongs not to the Will §.14–20.
[-§.21-] „But to the Agent or Man". §.21... the Question is not proper, whether the Will be free
but whether a Man be free... we can scarce tell how to imagine any Being freer, than
to be able to do what he wills...
„In respect of willing a Man is not free" §.22.... Concerning a Man's Liberty, there yet therefore
is raised this farther Question, Whether a Man be free to will? which I think, is what
is meant, when it is disputed, Whether the Will be free.... §.22–24. A Man in respect
of Willing, or the Act of Volition, when any Action in his Power is once proposed to his
Thoughts, as presently to be done, cannot be free...
„The will determined by something without it" §.25. Since then it is plain that in most
Cases a Man is not at Liberty, whether he will will; the next Thing demanded is, Whether
a Man be at Liberty to will which of the two he pleases, Motion or Rest. This Question
carries the Absurdity of it so manifestly in it self cc. (series infinita).
„What determines the will" §.29. The will being nothing but a Power in the Mind to direct
the operative Faculties of a Man to Motion or Rest, as far as they depend on such Direction.
To the Question, what is it determines the Will? the true and proper Answer is the
Mind.... If this Answer satisfies not, 'tis plain the Meaning of the Question, What
determines the Will? is this, What moves the Mind in every particular Instance,
to determine its general Power of directing to this or that particular Motion or
Rest? And to this I answer, The Motive for continuing in the same State or
Action, is only the present Satisfaction in it: The Motive to change, is always some Uneasi
ness: Nothing setting us upon the Change of State, or upon any new Action, but some
Uneasiness.... §.37 (s. o.) §.39. I have hitherto instanced in the Uneasiness of Desire,
as that which determines the Will... But yet we are not to look upon the Uneasiness
which makes up, or at least accompanies most of the other Passions, as wholly exclu
ded in the case. Aversion, Fear, Anger, Envy, Shame cc have each their Uneasiness too
and thereby influence the will... Nay, there is, I think, scarce any of the Passions to be
found without Desire joined with it. I am sure where-ever there is Uneasiness, there
is Desire...
